title: How A Simple List Can Improve Behavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a brief daily ritual for accelerating behavioral improvement: whenever a routine or activity doesn't go as expected, the teacher jots a short phrase on a sticky note (e.g., "getting into groups") and sets it aside without confronting students in the moment. The next morning, after opening with something genuinely positive, the teacher reads the accumulated list aloud, framing it neutrally as shared goals for the day rather than a rehash of the previous day's failures. He stresses the list should stay brief — no more than three items — and be delivered matter-of-factly, since its impersonal, list-based framing is what makes students receptive rather than defensive. Used consistently, he argues, this thirty-to-forty-five-second habit keeps students focused on continual improvement and eventually becomes unnecessary as the list runs out of items.
points: Daily ritual: jot a short phrase on a sticky note whenever a routine goes poorly, without confronting students about it in the moment.
The next morning, open with something genuinely positive before reading the accumulated list aloud as shared goals, not a rehash of failures.
Keep the list to no more than three items, delivered matter-of-factly in under a minute.
The list's impersonal, non-confrontational framing is what makes students receptive to it rather than defensive.
quotes: This week I’d like to share with you a very simple strategy.
The way it works is that you’re going to create a short daily list of anything you’re unsatisfied with.

As soon as your students are back and working in groups the way they were taught, you’re going to jot down on a sticky note or half sheet of paper a reminder to yourself that they had trouble with this one particular activity.
Now, it’s important to point out that you’re not doing this as a means of reprimanding your students. It isn’t a list of lecture points.
Then matter-of-factly tell them what areas you want to see improved that day. Keep it no more than three items and be brief.
Because it’s read off an impersonal list—like it’s something you’re all working on together—they respect it.
You’ll see progress day after day until one morning you’ll hold up your list, shrug your shoulders, and say, “I’ve got nothing. Let’s have another great day!
